title: Ezekiel 34:25–31
context: The LORD promises, “I will make with them a covenant of peace” (34:25). Harmful animals will cease, and the people will dwell securely even in the wilderness and the woods. The LORD will send “showers of blessing” in their season (34:26), the land will yield its fruit, and he will break “the bars of their yoke” (34:27). They will no longer be prey to the nations or suffer famine and the shame of the nations (34:28–29). The chapter closes with the covenant relationship: “they, the house of Israel, are my people” (34:30), and “You my sheep, the sheep of my pasture, are men, and I am your God” (34:31). The covenant of peace returns in 37:26, where it is called “an everlasting covenant”. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: a promise of security, plenty, and the LORD’s presence, given by grace to a restored people. Readers differ on how much of the imagery describes the return from exile, the age of the church, or the final new creation, and many read it on more than one level; this is not a fork between the two traditions.

verses.text: “ ‘I will make with them a covenant of peace, and will cause evil animals to cease out of the land. They will dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will make with them a covenant of peace, and will cause evil animals to cease out of the land.” Arminian readers note that the LORD’s covenant brings safety to a people who had been “food to all the animals” in 34:5. The flock can now “sleep in the woods.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the covenant of peace as the LORD’s gracious initiative, reversing the dangers of exile. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with 37:26, where the covenant of peace is called “an everlasting covenant”, and both see its fullness in the new covenant.

verses.text: I will make them and the places around my hill a blessing. I will cause the shower to come down in its season. There will be showers of blessing.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will make them and the places around my hill a blessing. I will cause the shower to come down in its season.” Arminian readers note that the people become a blessing, recalling the promise to Abraham. “There will be showers of blessing.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s blessing flowing from his presence at “my hill”, commonly taken as Zion. Shared ground: both traditions read the rain in its season as covenant blessing, the reverse of the drought and curse of the covenant warnings.

verses.text: The tree of the field will yield its fruit, and the earth will yield its increase, and they will be secure in their land. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bars of their yoke, and have delivered them out of the hand of those who made slaves of them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have broken the bars of their yoke”. Arminian readers note the language of deliverance from slavery, recalling the exodus. The LORD frees his people from “those who made slaves of them.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a new exodus, with the LORD breaking the yoke as he did in Egypt (compare Leviticus 26:13). Shared ground: both traditions read the fruitful land and the broken yoke together as the LORD’s act of redemption, leading to knowledge of him.

verses.text: They will no more be a prey to the nations, neither will the animals of the earth devour them; but they will dwell securely, and no one will make them afraid.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will no more be a prey to the nations,” but “they will dwell securely, and no one will make them afraid.” Arminian readers note that the flock once scattered and devoured now rests in safety. Fear gives way to peace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the promise of security as the work of the LORD who shepherds his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the phrase “no one will make them afraid” as a picture of covenant peace, and both see it reversing the losses described in 34:5–8.

verses.text: I will raise up to them a plantation for renown, and they will no more be consumed with famine in the land, and not bear the shame of the nations any more.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will raise up to them a plantation for renown, and they will no more be consumed with famine in the land”. Arminian readers note that the LORD removes both hunger and “the shame of the nations”. The people’s disgrace is replaced with honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD providing abundantly and restoring his people’s reputation among the nations. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the covenant blessings, hedging the precise sense of “a plantation for renown” while agreeing on its picture of fruitfulness.

verses.text: They will know that I, the LORD, their God am with them, and that they, the house of Israel, are my people, says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will know that I, the LORD, their God am with them, and that they, the house of Israel, are my people”. Arminian readers note that the goal of every blessing is the LORD’s presence and a restored relationship with his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the covenant formula, “my people,” as the heart of the promise, grounded in the LORD’s faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as stating plainly what the shepherd imagery has pictured: the LORD with his people, and his people belonging to him.

verses.text: You my sheep, the sheep of my pasture, are men, and I am your God,’ says the Lord GOD.”
verses.arminianNotes: “You my sheep, the sheep of my pasture, are men, and I am your God”. Arminian readers note that the shepherd image is explained: the sheep are people, and the LORD is their God. The chapter ends with relationship, not only with provision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of sheep and pasture interpreted as the covenant bond between the LORD and his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing verse, like Psalm 100:3, as a confession that God’s people belong to him and are cared for by him.
